name: Human Anatomy
purpose: A starting subject map for a Human Anatomy YouTube channel. Categories organize concrete subtopics; each entry supplies an episode question, a research outline and a boundary for case selection. Counts follow the authored coverage, with no imposed topic maximum.

topics.question: Why do anatomy diagrams show a standard body when real bodies vary?
topics.coverage: Compare reference orientation, proportions, normal variation and educational simplification without diagnostic judgments.

topics.question: How do bones, muscles and connective tissues share the work of moving a joint?
topics.coverage: Trace leverage, force transmission and stability conceptually; exclude exercise or rehabilitation prescriptions.

topics.question: How are pressure, flow and resistance related in the circulatory system?
topics.coverage: Use an explicit simplified model and distinguish it from personal blood-pressure interpretation.

topics.question: Why can the same organ look different across imaging methods and slice orientations?
topics.coverage: Compare planes, contrast mechanisms, resolution and movement; exclude image diagnosis.

topics.question: What did the National Library of Medicine's Visible Human Project make visible in its 1994–95 body image sets?
topics.coverage: Trace the publicly released male and female cadaver datasets, CT, MRI and cryosectional images and their use as anatomy references; distinguish two donor bodies and processed sections from population-wide normal anatomy, clinical diagnosis or live motion.

topics.question: How do heart valves coordinate one-way blood flow without actively pumping it?
topics.coverage: Trace pressure differences, valve structure and cardiac phases conceptually; exclude diagnosis.

topics.question: How does the kidney's microscopic structure separate filtration from selective recovery?
topics.coverage: Trace glomeruli, tubules, blood supply and concentration in a simplified model.

topics.question: Why does the lung divide gas-exchange space into many small units?
topics.coverage: Compare area, diffusion distance, ventilation, blood flow and structural support without medical interpretation.

topics.question: How do peripheral nerves carry sensory and motor information through one limb?
topics.coverage: Map nerve bundles, branches and mixed functions; distinguish anatomical overview from symptom localization.

topics.question: How do the digestive tract's layers coordinate propulsion, secretion and absorption in different segments?
topics.coverage: Trace wall structure, muscle, mucosa, ducts and blood or lymphatic routes in a labeled anatomical comparison; exclude diagnosis or dietary advice.

topics.question: Why can an endocrine gland influence a distant organ without a direct nerve connection?
topics.coverage: Map gland location, vascular access, target receptors and feedback anatomy using one illustrative axis; distinguish structural overview from individual hormone interpretation.

topics.question: How do lymphatic vessels and nodes connect fluid return with immune surveillance?
topics.coverage: Trace tissue fluid, vessels, valves, nodes and drainage territories; distinguish schematic drainage from diagnosing a swelling or predicting spread.

health.requirements: Inspect current professional guidance and original studies for the exact population, intervention or measurement. Report comparators, absolute outcomes, uncertainty, harms and limits. Do not diagnose, prescribe or imply that education replaces professional care.
source_leads: current official clinical or public-health guidance
original trials, cohort studies or diagnostic-validation reports
study registrations, protocols and adverse-event records

overlap_policy: The following homes have deliberately related subject matter. They are navigation leads, not proof that the same question belongs in every bank. Choose one primary home for an actual episode and link it elsewhere. Where a subject appears in more than one context, retain the distinct case, population, system or interpretive question.
handoff: Keep the BANK ID in notes. Refine the research question with an exact text edition, jurisdiction, population, product version, place, time range or clearly labeled fictional premise.
Inspect actual sources; no source was verified by generating this map. Apply the existing registry planning and idea readiness process before project creation.
Choose a current registered angle only after reading its niche-specific scope. This initial map has not checked or assigned angle plans for these entries.
Keep Q1-Q42, CAT defaults, project snapshots, output locations and production gates unchanged. Catalog counts are not production or publication counts.
Review neighboring banks for semantic overlap and follow the existing Phase 1 claim-ledger requirements. Add qualified review when required by the production contract.
coverage_limits: This initial map does not exhaust the niche, its regions, time periods, named case studies, texts, technical variants or disputed questions. It has not performed source-feasibility checks, semantic duplicate review of every pair, trend analysis, claim verification or episode production. Expand any category freely after identifying a real coverage gap; add categories where the subject requires them. Preserve existing IDs when refining wording and allocate new IDs only for genuinely new proposals.

# Human Anatomy Channel Master Topic Roadmap (Scratch to Advanced)
**Niche:** 352 Human Anatomy (Life_Biology)  
**Channel Language:** English (YouTube)  
**Target Audience:** Human Anatomy Researchers, Domain Specialists, Documentary Viewers, General Public (Global)  
**Production Format:** 10 to 30-Minute In-Depth Documentary Explainer Episodes (600s–1800s, 75–225 Fixed 8s Scenes)  
**Execution & Sync Report:** [topics/352_human_anatomy/TOPICS_COVERED_REPORT.md](./TOPICS_COVERED_REPORT.md)  

---

## 1. Channel Progression Strategy

This curriculum organizes the core disciplines of Human Anatomy across four progressive tiers:
- **Tier 1: Human Anatomy Foundations & Core Mechanisms (Beginner / Scratch)** — Core physical and conceptual fundamentals, terminology, primary mechanisms, and foundational observation methods in Human Anatomy.
- **Tier 2: Human Anatomy Methodological Deep Dives & Empirical Evidence (Intermediate)** — Detailed instrumentation, measurement metrics, classification systems, and documented case studies of Human Anatomy.
- **Tier 3: Human Anatomy Advanced Systemic Paradigms & Comparative Dynamics (Upper Intermediate)** — Complex systemic interactions, historical shifts, anomalous patterns, and comparative analyses across different contexts in Human Anatomy.
- **Tier 4: Human Anatomy Frontier Technologies, Global Impact & Future Horizons (Advanced / Masterclass)** — Emerging technological breakthroughs, policy frameworks, environmental and human impact, and long-term evolutionary projections for Human Anatomy.

---

## 3. Topic Catalog (Scratch to Advanced Curriculum)

### Tier 1: Foundational Frameworks
1. **The Architecture of Human Anatomy: A Body Structure First Described**
   - *Question:* Which observation changed a named anatomical account?
   - *Key Focus:* Use dated dissection, imaging, and terminology records. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
2. **Human Anatomy: A Textbook Diagram Rechecked**
   - *Question:* Which structures and variations does one familiar image omit?
   - *Key Focus:* Compare atlas with documented human samples. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
3. **Human Anatomy: People Behind Anatomical Knowledge**
   - *Question:* Who donated bodies, prepared specimens, drew atlases, and taught?
   - *Key Focus:* Trace consent, credit, and historical context. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
4. **Human Anatomy: Location, Structure, and Function**
   - *Question:* Where is one organ and how does its shape support a task?
   - *Key Focus:* Use accepted terminology and a bounded example. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
5. **Human Anatomy: Variation Is Part of Anatomy**
   - *Question:* How often does a named arrangement vary across people?
   - *Key Focus:* Check sample, imaging method, and population. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
### Tier 2: Methodological Deep Dives
6. **Human Anatomy: An Unclear Anatomical Image**
   - *Question:* Which variant or imaging artifact explains a structure?
   - *Key Focus:* Compare modalities and avoid individual diagnosis. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
7. **Human Anatomy: A New Anatomy Imaging Method**
   - *Question:* What detail became visible and what remained hidden?
   - *Key Focus:* Compare resolution, contrast, and validation. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
8. **Human Anatomy: An Anatomy Atlas's Authors**
   - *Question:* Who decided what counted as typical anatomy?
   - *Key Focus:* Read source specimens, editorial choices, and omissions. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
9. **Human Anatomy: A Terminology Revision**
   - *Question:* What structure name changed and why?
   - *Key Focus:* Use dated anatomical standards and professional discussion. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
10. **Human Anatomy: An Organ System in Motion**
   - *Question:* How do structure and neighboring tissues enable function?
   - *Key Focus:* Use measured anatomy and physiology. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
### Tier 3: Advanced Analytical Paradigms
11. **Human Anatomy: An Anatomical Belief Corrected**
   - *Question:* Which new observation overturned an earlier description?
   - *Key Focus:* Compare original and later evidence. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
12. **Human Anatomy: Studying Anatomy Across Eras**
   - *Question:* How did dissection, microscopy, and imaging alter one claim?
   - *Key Focus:* Compare what each method could measure. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
13. **Human Anatomy: A New Human Atlas**
   - *Question:* What populations and variations must it represent?
   - *Key Focus:* Specify sampling, consent, resolution, and access. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
14. **Human Anatomy: Everyone Has the Same Body Map?**
   - *Question:* Which normal variants complicate a single diagram?
   - *Key Focus:* Use prevalence-aware, neutral terminology. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
15. **Human Anatomy: A Specimen Becomes an Atlas Image**
   - *Question:* How did collection, consent, imaging, annotation, and teaching occur?
   - *Key Focus:* Follow provenance and rights. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
### Tier 4: Frontier Systems & Interdisciplinary Paradigms
16. **Human Anatomy: An Image to an Anatomical Claim**
   - *Question:* Which landmarks support a structure label?
   - *Key Focus:* Check orientation, scale, and expert validation. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
17. **Human Anatomy: Measuring an Organ**
   - *Question:* Which imaging or specimen method produced a dimension?
   - *Key Focus:* Report body position, age range, and uncertainty. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
18. **Human Anatomy: Anatomy Through Development**
   - *Question:* How does a structure change with age or condition?
   - *Key Focus:* Use defined population and time period. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
19. **Human Anatomy: Atlas and Living Body**
   - *Question:* How do preserved specimens differ from in vivo imaging?
   - *Key Focus:* Compare tissue state, posture, and motion. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.
20. **Human Anatomy: Normal Range of Structures**
   - *Question:* Which variants occur without pathology?
   - *Key Focus:* Use population data and avoid personal conclusions. Evidence base: NIH anatomical reference resources, consented specimen and imaging studies, terminology standards, atlas provenance, and population variation research.

prior_initial_map.overlap_policy: The following homes have deliberately related subject matter. They are navigation leads, not proof that the same question belongs in every bank. Choose one primary home for an actual episode and link it elsewhere. Where a subject appears in more than one context, retain the distinct case, population, system or interpretive question.
handoff: Keep the BANK ID in notes. Refine the research question with an exact text edition, jurisdiction, population, product version, place, time range or clearly labeled fictional premise.
Inspect actual sources; no source was verified by generating this map. Apply the existing registry planning and idea readiness process before project creation.
Choose a current registered angle only after reading its niche-specific scope. This initial map has not checked or assigned angle plans for these entries.
Keep Q1-Q42, CAT defaults, project snapshots, output locations and production gates unchanged. Catalog counts are not production or publication counts.
Review neighboring banks for semantic overlap and follow the existing Phase 1 claim-ledger requirements. Add qualified review when required by the production contract.
prior_initial_map.coverage_limits: This initial map does not exhaust the niche, its regions, time periods, named case studies, texts, technical variants or disputed questions. It has not performed source-feasibility checks, semantic duplicate review of every pair, trend analysis, claim verification or episode production. Expand any category freely after identifying a real coverage gap; add categories where the subject requires them. Preserve existing IDs when refining wording and allocate new IDs only for genuinely new proposals.
